cues.text: Ignatius of Antioch, c. AD 107
Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, was arrested during the reign of the emperor Trajan and marched under guard toward Rome, where he was martyred.

Along the way he wrote seven surviving letters, mostly to churches in Asia Minor, as well as one to the church at Rome and one to Polycarp, among the earliest Christian writings outside the New Testament itself.
Writing against believers who denied Christ had come in real human flesh, Ignatius pointed to the Eucharist as evidence against them.
They refuse it, he wrote, because they confess not the Eucharist to be the flesh of our Savior Jesus Christ.
For Ignatius the reality of the Eucharist and the reality of the Incarnation stood or fell together.
Justin Martyr, c. AD 150
Justin, a Christian philosopher later martyred in Rome, addressed his First Apology directly to the emperor, explaining Christian belief and practice to a largely hostile pagan readership.
His account of the Eucharist is one of the earliest full descriptions of the Mass to survive.
Christians do not receive ordinary bread and wine, Justin explained, but food that has become the flesh and blood of that Jesus who was made flesh.
Writing for outsiders with every reason to soften a strange-sounding claim, he stated it plainly instead.
Irenaeus of Lyons, c. AD 180
A bishop in Gaul, Irenaeus had heard St.
Polycarp — himself a disciple of the apostle John — preach in his own youth.
He wrote at length against the Gnostic teachers of his day, who taught that the material world was fundamentally corrupt and unworthy of God.
Irenaeus turned the Eucharist itself into an argument against them: Christ, he wrote, was exhibiting to us His true flesh in the Eucharist, conferring on our own flesh the capacity for salvation.
If ordinary bread and wine can become the Lord's own Body, matter cannot be the worthless thing the Gnostics claimed.
Cyril of Jerusalem, c. AD 350
Two centuries later, Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem, instructed newly baptized Christians in a series of mystagogical lectures delivered during Easter week.
Several are devoted entirely to the Eucharist, addressed to men and women about to receive it for the first time.
Cyril told his catechumens not to judge by taste, since the senses report only bread and wine, but to hold with unwavering faith that they receive the Body and Blood of Christ.

Coming from a bishop teaching ordinary new believers rather than defending the faith to outsiders, his lectures show the doctrine was the Church's common, taught belief — not a specialist's private theory.
A Continuous Witness
Four writers, four different centuries, four different purposes: a bishop under armed guard, a philosopher addressing an emperor, a theologian countering heresy, a pastor instructing new converts.
And one consistent claim running through all of them, decades and then centuries before Lanciano, before Bolsena, before any account gathered elsewhere in this exhibition.
The miracles are not where this belief began.
